Search Engine Marketing for Multifamily: One Renter, Four Places to Find You

Nov 2, 2026Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM

Search engine marketing for multifamily is everything that decides whether your community appears when a renter searches for a place to live: paid ads, organic results, Google Maps and AI answers. Those four should run as one system, because one renter can see all of them in a single sitting and will notice when the stories do not match.

Most portfolios do not buy it that way. SEO sits with one vendor, Google Ads with another, the Google Business Profile with a busy onsite team, and nobody owns the AI answers. Each one reports its own wins. I read this kind of reporting every week, and the costly problem I keep finding is four channels courting the same renter with different facts.

Why does a renter's search need one system?

Look at how the search starts. In an Apartments.com survey of more than 15,000 US renters, reported by the National Apartment Association, 87% said they did not have a specific property in mind when they began. The average renter planned to research 10 properties and seriously consider three. 85% said they use or plan to use a listing site, which you should weigh knowing a listing site ran the survey. Search engines came in at 35%.

Zillow reports that the typical renter used five different sites or apps during the search. So the same person may meet your ad, your Maps listing and an AI summary within an evening. If the ad says six weeks free, the profile says eight and the AI answer quotes last year's rent, nobody calls to complain. You stay on the list of ten and miss the three, and no report will show it.

What does each surface actually do?

Paid search rents a position

Ads show up the day you turn them on and vanish the day you stop. That makes them the right tool for a new community with no search history, or for a floor plan that has to move this month. They are also the fastest way to test whether a message gets a response. We go deeper on that in our post on when multifamily Google Ads earn their budget.

Organic search builds the record

Your website takes longer to earn its place, and it keeps working when the budget pauses. It also carries more weight than it used to, because Google says a page must be indexed to appear as a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode. The site that answers renter questions is feeding two surfaces at once.

Google Maps cannot be bought

Google says local results come down to relevance, distance and prominence, and that "there's no way to request or pay for a better local ranking." Because no budget line protects it, Maps is often the first surface to drift when nobody clearly owns it. Our earlier piece on winning in Google Maps covers why it deserves its own attention.

AI answers shrink the list

AI tools are a small part of the renter search today. Only 5% of renters in that same survey named AI chatbots. What matters more is what happens to the links when a summary appears. In a Pew Research Center analysis of March 2025 browsing data from 900 US adults, people clicked a traditional search result on 8% of visits with an AI summary and on 15% of visits without one. Those were general Google searches, so read them as direction, and remember a community can rank on Google and still go unnamed in ChatGPT.

Where do the four surfaces break each other?

  • Specials drift. Apartment List put the national concession rate, the share of properties advertising at least a month free, at 31.3% in September 2026, up from 25.4% a year earlier. More offers means more changes, and each one has to land everywhere. We regularly find one page of a property site telling a different version of the deal than the next.
  • Money goes to the name you already own. Ads on your own community name can look great in a report while the unbranded searches, where renters with no property in mind start, sit untouched.
  • What renters ask never travels. The search terms from the ad account and the questions asked on the phone seldom reach whoever writes the website.
  • Everyone claims the lease. A renter who saw an ad, read reviews on Maps and then typed your name gets counted by three vendors. A lease is always a combination, and a report that pretends otherwise makes budget decisions harder.

How should the budget split between them?

Anyone who gives you a universal percentage has not looked at your community. The split follows the stage you are in.

A lease up leans on paid search early, since it has few reviews and little history for Google to weigh, while the organic and Maps work is built underneath it. A stabilized community should have earned enough free visibility that paid search becomes a targeted tool, aimed at the plans with real exposure. The useful question each month is which surface is carrying the load and which one should be carrying more next quarter.

What does running it as one system look like?

You do not have to hire one agency. You do need one owner. Someone has to hold the current facts for each community, see all four surfaces on the same page, and decide what changes this week.

A simple test: ask each vendor to send you today's special, the starting rent for your most available floor plan, and the renter question they most recently acted on. Compare the answers side by side. The differences are your gap list.

In our own work this is what LocalLift is for. It brings Google profile work, Maps visibility and AI discovery under one roof, and our multifamily marketing team runs social and paid media beside it, so every piece sends the same signal. A Weekly Pulse then gives the property one read on all of it. We do this for lease ups and established communities in five states, and the aim is simple: nobody on your side should have to referee between vendors.

How do you measure it without double counting?

Keep one scoreboard per community, and separate what each surface can prove. Paid search can show cost per qualified call. Organic can show how often you appear for searches that do not include your name. Maps can show where you hold ground and where you lose it across your actual trade area. AI can show whether tools name you and whether what they say is true. Tours and leases sit at the bottom as the shared result that no single channel gets to claim.

Questions we hear

What is search engine marketing for apartments?

It is the combined work of showing up when renters search: paid ads, organic results, Google Maps and AI answers. Many vendors use the term to mean paid ads alone, so ask which one a proposal covers.

Is SEM the same as Google Ads?

Often it is used that way, and that is the trap. If your SEM line only covers ads, the other three places renters look may have no owner.

Should a stabilized community keep running paid search?

Sometimes. It earns its place when specific floor plans have exposure or a nearby rival has changed the market. Running it at a flat level all year, mostly on your own name, is harder to defend.

Do AI answers matter yet for apartments?

They are small but worth watching. Survey shares are still small, and AI summaries can reduce clicks to the links beneath them. Checking whether the answers are accurate is a sensible first step.

Do we need one agency for all four?

No. You need one accountable owner and one set of facts. A single team makes that easier, but several vendors can work if someone holds them to the same page.
